hero.title: Electricity — Ohm's Law & Circuits Made Simple
hero.hook: Every device you plug in, every bulb that glows, every phone that charges — all of it comes down to three quantities: Voltage, Current, and Resistance. And one elegant law connecting them. Master Ohm's Law and you unlock the entire Electricity chapter.

hook_section.scenario: You have a torch with fresh batteries — bright light. Put old, weak batteries in — dim light. Same bulb, same wire, different voltage. The current flowing through the bulb changes with voltage. And the bulb's resistance stays the same. This is Ohm's Law in action — every single day, in every device you own.
hook_section.bridge: Electricity is Class 10 Science's highest-weightage chapter — typically 7–8 marks in the board exam. Ohm's Law, series/parallel circuits, and the heating effect are almost always tested together.
hook_section.punchline: V = IR. This one equation, with its three arrangements, can answer almost every Electricity question.

concept_section.analogy: Think of electricity like water in a pipe. Voltage is water pressure (pushes water through). Current is how fast water flows. Resistance is how narrow or rough the pipe is. More pressure (V) → more flow (I). Narrower pipe (R) → less flow. That's exactly V = IR.
concept_section.principle: Ohm's Law: V = IR (Voltage = Current × Resistance). Three forms: I = V/R, R = V/I. Series: R_total = R₁+R₂+... | Parallel: 1/R_total = 1/R₁+1/R₂+...
concept_section.reveal_prompt: Tap each circuit type to compare them 👇

reveals.question: 🔗 Series Circuit — key facts?
reveals.answer: Same current through all components. Total voltage = sum of individual voltages. Total resistance = R₁+R₂+R₃. If one component fails, the whole circuit breaks (like old Christmas lights).

reveals.question: ⚡ Parallel Circuit — key facts?
reveals.answer: Same voltage across all components. Total current = sum of individual currents. Total resistance is LESS than any single resistance. If one branch fails, others keep working (like home wiring).

reveals.question: 🌡️ Heating Effect of Current?
reveals.answer: Heat produced H = I²Rt (Joule's Law). More current, more resistance, more time → more heat. Used in: electric heater, bulb, iron, toaster. This is why high-current devices need thick wires.

reveals.question: 💡 Electric Power?
reveals.answer: P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Unit: Watt (W). A 60W bulb uses 60 joules per second. Energy = P × t (in joules) or in kWh for billing. 1 kWh = 1 unit of electricity.

points: Ohm's Law: V = IR — valid for metallic conductors at constant temperature
Series: R_total = R₁+R₂, same current; Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁+1/R₂, same voltage
Resistance factors: R ∝ length, R ∝ 1/area, depends on material (ρ); R = ρl/A
Joule's heating: H = I²Rt — basis of all heating appliances
Electric power: P = VI; Energy = Pt; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J

exam_questions.question: Three resistors 2Ω, 3Ω, 6Ω are connected in parallel. Find (a) total resistance (b) current from 6V battery
A wire of resistance 10Ω is stretched to double its length. What is its new resistance?
State Ohm's Law and write its mathematical form

quiz.q: Three resistors 6Ω, 3Ω, 2Ω are in parallel. Total resistance is:
quiz.exp: 1/R = 1/6+1/3+1/2 = 1/6+2/6+3/6 = 6/6 = 1. So R = 1Ω. Parallel resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance.

quiz.q: A wire of resistance R is stretched to twice its length. New resistance is:
quiz.exp: R = ρl/A. Doubling length also halves area (same volume). New R = ρ(2l)/(A/2) = 4R.

quiz.q: Heating effect of current is used in:
quiz.exp: Electric iron uses Joule heating (H = I²Rt). Motors and generators convert electrical to mechanical energy; bells use electromagnetic effects.

quiz.q: In a series circuit with two bulbs, if one bulb fuses:
quiz.exp: In series, all components share the same current path. If one breaks, the circuit is open — no current flows anywhere.

flipcards.back: V = IR — voltage across a conductor is directly proportional to current through it, at constant temperature

flipcards.front: Series vs Parallel — which has higher resistance?
flipcards.back: Series — resistances add up. Parallel — total resistance is less than smallest individual resistance.
H = I²Rt — Heat = current² × resistance × time

flipcards.front: How does resistance depend on length?
flipcards.back: R ∝ l (directly proportional). Double the length → double the resistance

flipcards.front: Why is home wiring done in parallel?
flipcards.back: Each appliance gets full voltage independently; one failure doesn't affect others
